description.value: This study examined whether subjective responses to alcohol during laboratory alcohol administration predict neural responses to alcohol taste cues during fMRI in alcohol-dependent participants, including moderation by OPRM1 genotype.

spans.text: The primary aim of this study was to integrate human laboratory methods with neuroimaging by testing whether subjective responses to alcohol during alcohol administration predict neural responses to alcohol cues in the scanner.

description.value: A within-subjects study of alcohol-dependent participants who completed controlled intravenous alcohol administration in the laboratory followed approximately one week later by an fMRI alcohol taste-cue task.

spans.text: Twenty of the 43 individuals then went on to the neuroimaging portion of the study approximately 1 week following the last infusion.

The primary aim of this study was to integrate human laboratory methods with neuroimaging by testing whether subjective responses to alcohol during alcohol administration predict neural responses to alcohol cues in the scanner.

value: The alcohol- versus water-cues contrast activated a broad set of regions including mesocorticolimbic areas, limbic cortex (insula, posterior cingulate gyrus), parietal lobe (precuneus), thalamus, and occipital areas.
These results suggest that subjective responses to alcohol during alcohol administration predict specific patterns of brain activation during alcohol cue exposure.

spans.text: Consistent with the previous studies of the alcohol cues task, and as reported by Ray and colleagues (2013b) , the alcohol- versus water-cues contrast activated a broad set of regions including mesocorticolimbic areas, limbic cortex (insula, posterior cingulate gyrus), parietal lobe (precuneus), thalamus, and occipital areas ( Table 3 ).

value: The baseline-corrected average craving scores across BrAC were found to negatively correlate with the neural response to alcohol cues in the postcentral gyrus, precuneus, posterior cingulate gyrus, and lingual gyrus regions. No positive correlation was found.

This triangular finding suggests that the expanded item set and the use of the full Likert rating scale to assess craving in the laboratory allowed for the acquisition of more meaningful variance from which the association with brain activity could be detected.

value: There was a positive correlation between average alcohol high reported across BrAC and neural response to alcohol cues in the pre- and postcentral gyri, precuneus, anterior cingulate cortex, and supplementary motor cortex. No negative correlation was found.
Alcohol high predicted greater neural activity to alcohol cues in regions including the precuneus and anterior cingulate cortex.

spans.text: There was a positive correlation between average alcohol high reported across BrAC and neural response to alcohol cues in the pre- and postcentral gyri, precuneus, anterior cingulate cortex, and supplementary motor cortex ( Table 5 ). No significant correlation between alcohol liking and neural response to alcohol cues was observed.

spans.text: Further, a positive correlation was observed between scores on the negative reinforcement factor (where more negative scores reflect greater reductions in tension and negative mood compared with baseline) and some of these same regions (the precuneus, posterior cingulate, and lingual gyrus) ( Table 7 , Figure 3 ).
